title: CI/CD for Machine Learning
summary: Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment automate the path from code change to running system. For ML, CI/CD tests your code and data, retrains or validates models, and deploys them automatically when checks pass. GitHub Actions is a popular
content:
# CI/CD for Machine Learning ##### The Friday deploy that served random predictions An engineer pushed a "small refactor" to a churn model service on a Friday afternoon. They had renamed a feature column from `tenure_months` to `tenure` for consistency, updated the training script, and deployed. The training script was fine. The **serving code** still built its feature frame with the old column name. scikit-learn's pipeline received a DataFrame whose columns did not match what the ColumnTransformer expected, silently filled the missing column, and returned predictions that were essentially noise. No test caught it, because there were no tests. No deployment gate caught it, because deployment was `scp` and a restart. The service returned 200 for every request with a valid-looking probability, so no alert fired. It ran for four days. A single automated test — train, save, load, predict on a fixture, assert the output is sane — would have failed in twelve seconds. **CI/CD is what makes that test run whether or not anyone remembers.** ##### What CI/CD means for ML **Continuous Integration** — every push triggers automated checks. **Continuous Delivery/Deployment** — passing changes flow automatically to staging and, with a gate, to production. ML pipelines have all the usual stages plus concerns that DevOps does not address: | Stage | Traditional software | Additional for ML | |---|---|---| | Lint / format | Yes | Yes | | Unit tests | Yes | Plus **data quality** tests | | Integration tests | Yes | Plus **model contract** tests | | Build | Container image | Container **+ model artifact** | | Deploy | Application | Model **registry promotion** | | Post-deploy | Smoke test | **Prediction sanity** + drift baseline | | Trigger | Code push | Code push **+ data change + drift + schedule** | That last row is the structural difference: a traditional pipeline runs when code changes, while an ML pipeline may also need to run when *data* changes or when monitoring detects drift. ##### GitHub Actions basics A workflow is YAML in `.github/workflows/`. Three concepts: **jobs** run in parallel by default, **steps** run in sequence within a job, and **triggers** decide when. ```yaml name: CI on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] concurrency: # cancel superseded runs on the same branch group: ci-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: true jobs: quality: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.11" cache: pip # cache dependencies between runs - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt - run: ruff check . - run: ruff format --check . - run: mypy src/ ``` The `concurrency` block is worth including from the start — without it, pushing three commits in a minute queues three full runs, and you wait for all of them. ##### Testing ML code This is where ML pipelines differ most, and the tests fall into four categories. **Unit tests on deterministic logic** — feature engineering, preprocessing, and anything with a definite correct answer: ```python import pytest import pandas as pd from src.features import build_features, normalize_amount @pytest.mark.parametrize("raw,expected", [ ("₹1,299.00", 1299.00), ("1299", 1299.00), ("", None), (None, None), ]) def test_amount_parsing(raw, expected): assert normalize_amount(raw) == expected def test_feature_columns_are_stable(): """Guards against the exact bug from the opening story.""" df = pd.read_parquet("tests/fixtures/sample.parquet") features = build_features(df) expected = {"amount", "tenure_months", "prior_transactions", "merchant_category", "hour_of_day"} assert set(features.columns) == expected, "feature contract changed" ``` That second test is the one that would have caught the four-day incident. A **feature contract test** asserts that the column names and order your model expects have not changed, and it costs three lines. **Data quality tests** — schema, ranges, distributions: ```python def test_training_data_quality(): df = pd.read_parquet("data/features/train.parquet") assert not df.isna().any().any(), "nulls in training data" assert df["amount"].between(0, 1e7).all(), "amount out of range" assert df["label"].isin([0, 1]).all(), "invalid labels" positive_rate = df["label"].mean() assert 0.005 < positive_rate < 0.05, f"unexpected class balance: {positive_rate:.4f}" ``` The distribution assertion catches silent upstream changes — a data pipeline modification that doubles your positive rate should fail the build, not train a model on it. **Model contract tests** — behavioural guarantees on the trained artifact: ```python import joblib, numpy as np @pytest.fixture(scope="module") def model(): return joblib.load("models/model.joblib") def test_prediction_shape_and_range(model): X = pd.read_parquet("tests/fixtures/sample.parquet") probs = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] assert probs.shape == (len(X),) assert np.all((probs >= 0) & (probs <= 1)) def test_meets_minimum_performance(model): """A THRESHOLD test — statistical, not deterministic.""" X_test = pd.read_parquet("tests/fixtures/holdout_X.parquet") y_test = pd.read_parquet("tests/fixtures/holdout_y.parquet")["label"] from sklearn.metrics import f1_score score = f1_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)) assert score >= 0.82, f"F1 regressed to {score:.3f} (floor 0.82)" def test_no_regression_against_champion(model): """New model must not be meaningfully worse than the current production one.""" champion = joblib.load("models/champion.joblib") new_score = evaluate(model) old_score = evaluate(champion) assert new_score >= old_score - 0.01, \ f"regression: {new_score:.3f} vs champion {old_score:.3f}" def test_directional_behaviour(model): """Sanity: higher amount at 3am should not DECREASE fraud probability.""" base = make_transaction(amount=500, hour=14) risky = make_transaction(amount=95_000, hour=3) assert model.predict_proba(risky)[0, 1] > model.predict_proba(base)[0, 1] ``` The **threshold test** is the statistical analogue of a unit test — it can pass today and fail tomorrow with identical code, because the data changed. The **champion comparison** prevents deploying a model that trains successfully but performs worse than what is already live. **Serving tests** — the API contract: ```python from fastapi.testclient import TestClient from src.main import app client = TestClient(app) def test_predict_endpoint(): r = client.post("/v1/predict", json=VALID_PAYLOAD) assert r.status_code == 200 assert 0 <= r.json()["fraud_probability"] <= 1 def test_rejects_invalid_input(): r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={**VALID_PAYLOAD, "amount": -50}) assert r.status_code == 422 ``` ##### The full pipeline ```yaml name: CD on: push: branches: [main] tags: ["v*"] permissions: contents: read packages: write id-token: write # OIDC — no long-lived cloud keys jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest services: postgres: # real dependencies, not mocks image: postgres:16-alpine env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test, POSTGRES_DB: test } options: >- --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 10s --health-retries 5 ports: ["5432:5432"] steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: { python-version: "3.11", cache: pip } - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt - name: Pull versioned data run: dvc pull --run-cache env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }} AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }} - run: pytest tests/unit tests/data -q - run: pytest tests/model -q # threshold + contract tests - run: pytest tests/serving -q build: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest outputs: image: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - id: meta uses: docker/metadata-action@v5 with: images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/model-api tags: | type=sha,prefix=,format=short type=ref,event=tag - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: context: . push: true tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }} cache-from: type=gha # reuse layers across CI runs cache-to: type=gha,mode=max deploy-staging: needs: build runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: name: staging url: https://staging.example.com steps: - name: Deploy run: ./scripts/deploy.sh staging ${{ github.sha }} - name: Smoke test run: | curl -fsS --retry 8 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors \ https://staging.example.com/health/ready # Prediction sanity check — not just "is it up" RESULT=$(curl -fsS -X POST https://staging.example.com/v1/predict \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @tests/fixtures/known_case.json) echo "$RESULT" | python -c " import json,sys p = json.load(sys.stdin)['fraud_probability'] assert 0.6 < p < 1.0, f'known fraud case scored {p}' " deploy-production: needs: deploy-staging runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: name: production # ← required-reviewer gate configured here url: https://api.example.com steps: - name: Deploy run: ./scripts/deploy.sh production ${{ github.sha }} - name: Verify or roll back run: | if ! ./scripts/smoke_test.sh https://api.example.com; then echo "::error::Smoke test failed — rolling back" ./scripts/rollback.sh production exit 1 fi - name: Promote model in registry run: python scripts/promote_model.py --alias champion --sha ${{ github.sha }} ``` Three elements deserve emphasis. **The prediction sanity check** goes beyond "is the service up." It sends a known case and asserts the output is in the expected range — which is exactly what would have caught the noise-predictions incident, because a scrambled feature frame produces a probability nowhere near 0.6–1.0 for a known fraud case. **The approval gate** lives on the GitHub Environment, not in the YAML. Configure required reviewers in repository settings, and the job pauses until someone approves, with the decision recorded. **Automatic rollback** on smoke-test failure means a bad deploy self-heals before anyone reads the notification. ##### Continuous training triggers ML pipelines need triggers that code pipelines do not: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: "0 3 * * 1" # weekly retrain, Monday 03:00 UTC workflow_dispatch: # manual trigger with inputs inputs: reason: description: "Why are you retraining?" required: true repository_dispatch: types: [drift-detected] # fired by your monitoring system ``` The `repository_dispatch` trigger is the interesting one — your drift monitor detects a distribution shift and calls the GitHub API to start a retraining run: ```python import httpx def trigger_retrain(reason: str, metrics: dict) -> None: httpx.post( f"https://api.github.com/repos/{REPO}/dispatches", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {GH_TOKEN}", "Accept": "application/vnd.github+json"}, json={"event_type": "drift-detected", "client_payload": {"reason": reason, "metrics": metrics}}, timeout=15, ) ``` Critically, **automated retraining must not auto-deploy.** The pipeline trains, evaluates against thresholds, compares to the champion, and *registers* the candidate — then a human approves promotion. A retraining pipeline that deploys automatically will one day train on corrupted data and ship it. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Code push] --> B[Lint + type check] A2[Schedule / drift event] --> T[Retrain] B --> C[Unit + data quality tests] C --> D[Model contract tests
threshold + champion comparison] T --> D D -->|fails| X[Block — notify] D -->|passes| E[Build image
tagged with SHA] E --> F[Deploy staging
+ prediction sanity check] F --> G{{Manual approval
required reviewer}} G --> H[Deploy production] H --> I{Smoke test?} I -->|pass| J[Promote model alias
+ record baseline] I -->|fail| K[Automatic rollback] ``` ##### Handling data in CI Two practical problems. **Datasets are too large for CI** — a 2 GB pull on every run is slow and expensive. The fix is committed **fixtures**: a few hundred representative rows in `tests/fixtures/`, small enough for Git, sufficient for contract and shape tests. Pull the real data only in the training job. **Full training is too slow for CI.** A model taking two hours cannot run on every pull request. Split the workflows: fast tests on every PR, full training on schedule or manual trigger. ##### Common mistakes - **No feature contract test** — the four-day noise-prediction incident. - **No smoke test after deploy**, so a broken rollout looks successful. - **Testing only that the service is up**, not that predictions are sane. - **Automated retraining that auto-deploys** without evaluation gates or approval. - **Full datasets pulled in CI** rather than small committed fixtures. - **No champion comparison**, so a worse model can be promoted. - **Secrets echoed** into logs. - **No caching**, making CI slow enough that people bypass it. - **Deploying `latest`** rather than a SHA-tagged image, making rollback ambiguous. - **No approval gate** on production. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: create a **GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests and builds a Docker image** for your model API on every push. Include a feature contract test and a model threshold test — those two are what make it an *ML* pipeline rather than a generic one, and both are a few lines. The mini project is the **end-to-end pipeline**: test, build, and deploy your containerized model API automatically on push to main. Add the production environment with a required reviewer, and the automatic rollback on smoke-test failure. Then exercise the failure path deliberately — break the smoke test and confirm the rollback fires. A pipeline whose failure path you have never run is a pipeline you should not trust. For the assignment, **describe what a CI/CD pipeline for an ML project should test and automate, from commit to deployment**. Structure it by stage, and make the ML-specific additions explicit: data quality and distribution tests, feature contract tests, model performance thresholds, champion comparison, prediction sanity checks after deploy, and non-code triggers from drift or schedule. Use the renamed-column story to justify the feature contract test — a concrete failure that a three-line test prevents is more persuasive than a checklist. ##### Key takeaways - ML pipelines add data quality tests, feature contract tests and statistical performance thresholds to the usual lint-test-build-deploy sequence. - A feature contract test asserting column names and order catches the training/serving mismatch that silently produces garbage predictions. - Model tests are statistical — they can fail tomorrow with identical code — and should include a comparison against the current champion. - Smoke tests must verify prediction sanity, not just that the service responds, and failure should trigger automatic rollback. - Trigger retraining from schedules and drift events as well as commits, but never auto-deploy a retrained model without evaluation gates and human approval.
